deeper.title: Why amoxicillin works in otitis but fails in some urinary infections
deeper.html:
Amoxicillin kills E. coli only if the strain lacks a β-lactamase. Many community E. coli now carry one, so amoxicillin alone fails in a large share of urinary infections, while adding clavulanic acid (a suicide inhibitor) restores activity against the common enzymes. ESBL-producing strains, however, also destroy third-generation cephalosporins, and carbapenemase producers destroy almost everything. The choice of drug therefore follows the local resistance pattern and the culture result, which is why urine cultures matter when a first treatment fails.

Source: the lecture's penicillin A spectrum, β-lactamase inhibitors and ESBLs.

deeper.title: Why antibiotics barely change the cough
deeper.html:
By the time the typical whoop appears, the bacteria have already paralysed and destroyed ciliated cells and released toxins; many patients have cleared most bacteria by then. Antibiotics started in the paroxysmal stage therefore do little to shorten the cough, which lasts until the ciliated lining regenerates, but they still matter: they stop the patient spreading the infection to unvaccinated infants, in whom pertussis can cause apnoea and death. That is also why contacts are treated and pregnant women are offered a booster, so that antibodies cross the placenta.

Source: the lecture's clinical stages and treatment notes.

deeper.title: Why 'atypical' pneumonias ignore amoxicillin
deeper.html:
Amoxicillin, the standard first choice for community pneumonia, targets penicillin-binding proteins that build peptidoglycan. Chlamydia lacks a classical peptidoglycan wall and hides inside cells; Mycoplasma has no wall at all; Legionella lives inside macrophages. These 'atypical' organisms therefore need drugs that reach inside cells and act on ribosomes or DNA: macrolides, tetracyclines or fluoroquinolones. That is why a young adult with a dry cough and a pneumonia that does not improve on amoxicillin is often switched to a macrolide.

Source: the lecture's treatment notes and the Mycoplasma lecture.

deeper.title: Why hand hygiene beats new antibiotics
deeper.html:
Carbapenem-resistant Klebsiella leaves only a few toxic drugs such as colistin, and resistance to those is appearing. But the organism does not fly: in hospitals it travels on hands, stethoscopes, sinks and catheters from colonised to vulnerable patients. Cleaning hands at the WHO's five moments, isolating carriers and removing catheters as early as possible break that chain for every species at once, which is why infection control is often more powerful than any single new drug.

Source: the lecture's Klebsiella prevention table.

deeper.title: Typhoid Mary and the carrier state
deeper.html:
Mary Mallon, a cook in New York in the early 1900s, was healthy but carried S. Typhi in her gallbladder and infected dozens of people through the food she prepared. She became the classic example of the asymptomatic chronic carrier described in this lecture: bacteria shelter in the gallbladder, often around gallstones, and are shed in stool for years. This is why food handlers are screened, why typhoid is a notifiable disease and why carriers may need prolonged antibiotics or even cholecystectomy.

Source: history of public health; the lecture's carrier state.

deeper.title: How a hospital outbreak of resistance can cross species
deeper.html:
A carbapenemase gene on a conjugative plasmid does not stay with the Klebsiella that first carried it. In a patient's gut, the plasmid can pass by conjugation to E. coli, Enterobacter and other species, and a transposon or integron cassette can hop onto a different plasmid. Infection control teams therefore track the gene and plasmid, not just the species, and screening, isolation and restricting broad-spectrum antibiotics (which select the carriers) are the main defences.

Source: the lecture's mobile elements and conjugation.

deeper.title: Why 'influenzae' is a misnomer
deeper.html:
Richard Pfeiffer isolated this bacterium from patients during the 1889-1892 influenza pandemic and believed it caused the flu, hence the name. Only in 1933 was influenza shown to be a virus; H. influenzae had been a frequent secondary invader of lungs damaged by the virus. The same partnership still matters: a viral respiratory infection damages the ciliated epithelium and mucosal defences, opening the way to bacterial superinfection by H. influenzae, pneumococcus or S. aureus.

Source: history of microbiology; the lecture's pathogenesis steps.

deeper.title: Why antibiotics can cause diarrhoea
deeper.html:
The colon's resident flora is a biological barrier: it occupies space and nutrients and makes substances that suppress newcomers. A course of broad-spectrum antibiotics kills much of it, and Clostridioides difficile, whose spores survive the treatment, can then grow and release toxins that damage the colon, causing diarrhoea and sometimes pseudomembranous colitis. It is the clearest example in this lecture of mutualistic flora protecting us, and of how removing it lets an opportunist become a pathogen.

Source: the lecture's normal flora and opportunistic infection.

deeper.title: Why TB needs six months of treatment
deeper.html:
Most bacterial infections clear in days, but M. tuberculosis divides only every 15-20 hours and part of the population sits dormant inside granulomas and caseous material, barely metabolising. Drugs that kill actively dividing bacilli (isoniazid) act fast on the multiplying population, while rifampicin and pyrazinamide are needed to reach the slow and semi-dormant ones. Stopping early leaves survivors that cause relapse, often with acquired resistance, which is why adherence and directly observed therapy are central to TB control.

Source: the lecture's slow growth, latency and 2RHZE/4RH regimen.

deeper.title: The 'fried egg' colony
deeper.html:
Mycoplasma colonies are tiny, visible only with a magnifier, and look like a fried egg: a dense centre growing down into the agar with a thin, flat edge on the surface. The shape reflects their lack of a wall: the soft cells can push between agar fibres. Their size also explains why they pass through the 0.22 µm filters used to sterilise media, making them a common hidden contaminant of cell cultures in research laboratories.

Source: the lecture's size, culture media and cell-culture contamination.

deeper.title: Why pneumococcal colonies look like draughts pieces
deeper.html:
As a pneumococcal colony ages, the bacteria in its centre switch on their autolysin (LytA) and digest their own walls. The middle collapses while the edge keeps growing, giving a flat colony with a raised rim and sunken centre, the 'draughtsman' look. The same enzyme explains two lab tests: bile salts trigger autolysin, so the colony dissolves (bile solubility), and it releases pneumolysin, a key toxin, during infection. One enzyme links colony shape, diagnosis and virulence.

Source: the lecture's autolysin, bile solubility and colony description.

deeper.title: Why penicillin still works after 80 years
deeper.html:
Many bacteria became resistant to penicillin within years, yet group A streptococci have never been found resistant. Their resistance would require altered penicillin-binding proteins, and the changes that lower penicillin binding seem to cost the organism too much fitness to persist. Macrolide resistance, by contrast, spreads easily through efflux genes on mobile elements. This is why penicillin remains first line and why a macrolide given to an allergic patient may fail: know the local macrolide resistance rate before relying on it.

Source: the lecture's treatment table (no penicillin resistance; mef-mediated macrolide resistance).

deeper.title: Why the growth phase matters for antibiotics
deeper.html:
Many antibiotics, especially β-lactams, kill bacteria while they are building new wall, so they work best in the exponential phase. Bacteria in the stationary phase, or inside a biofilm where nutrients and oxygen are scarce, divide slowly and survive these drugs even without resistance genes (tolerance). That is why infections on catheters, prosthetic valves or joints relapse so often, and why they may need the device removed or long, combined treatment.

Source: the lecture's growth curve, slime layer and β-lactam mode of action.
